problem: Diffusion navigation world models such as NWM are trained with parallel supervision on ground-truth contexts but roll out autoregressively at inference on their own predictions. This train-test mismatch (exposure bias) makes long-horizon rollouts drift and degrades planning.
motivation: Reliable long-horizon imagination is needed for planning with world models, and even small rollout drift causes mis-ranked candidate trajectories. Existing fixes such as Self Forcing need distribution-matching losses, discriminators, or architecture changes, so a simple fix that keeps the standard diffusion loss and sampler is desirable.
key_idea: During training, roll the diffusion world model out autoregressively, append its own stop-gradient predicted x0 to the context at every step, and apply the unchanged single-step diffusion loss on those self-generated contexts.
insight: The gain comes from conditioning on the model's own rollout contexts, not from extra losses. It beats Self Forcing (distribution-matching) at 16s on most action-conditioned planning metrics, and the ablation on len_traj_pred (4/8/16) shows longer training rollouts steadily improve long-horizon LPIPS/DreamSim/FID. Gains are strongest at short-to-mid horizons; at 16s some metrics on HuRoN and SCAND get worse, so the effect is not uniform.
method: AR Forcing rollout training: during training the model autoregressively predicts up to 16 next frames (4 fps), and each step's prediction updates the context (sliding window of K=4 latents).
Context update: predicted x0 is reconstructed from epsilon via the standard inversion, x0_hat = (x_t - sqrt(1-abar)·eps_hat)/sqrt(abar), and appended to the context; no inner denoising loop.
Stop-gradient on rollout contexts: gradients do not flow through previous steps, so it acts as a DAgger-style approximation that saves memory and stabilizes training.

Unchanged objective: the loss is the standard single-step epsilon-MSE diffusion loss (with learned variance), computed under model-induced contexts p_theta; no discriminator, DMD, or architecture change.
Backbone/init: CDiT-XL/2 with Stable Diffusion VAE latents (28x28x4), initialized from the pretrained NWM checkpoint, AdamW lr 8e-5, total batch 96, 50k steps.
Planning: as in NWM, cross-entropy-method style planning: 120 candidate trajectories, top 5 used to update the action distribution, cost is LPIPS to the goal image, 8-step rollout.

setting.backbone: CDiT-XL/2 diffusion world model (initialized from NWM, fine-tuned with AR Forcing) + SD VAE
setting.training_data: RECON, TartanDrive, SCAND, HuRoN navigation datasets (same as NWM); Go Stanford held out for zero-shot
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB, 4 context frames at 224x224, plus relative actions from pose
setting.action_space: relative 2D translation + yaw between frames (normalized by per-dataset step length); planning over candidate trajectories
setting.privileged: goal image observation; ground-truth poses used for action conditioning and evaluation

numbers.evidence: Table A1_metrics, Goal-Conditioned Visual Navigation 4s/8s/16s, RECON row

numbers.extra: 2s horizon (aggregate over datasets); goal-conditioned visual navigation
numbers.evidence: Table ate_rte, Comparison on Goal-Conditioned Visual Navigation for 2 seconds

numbers_note: No standard VLN/ObjectNav benchmarks; results are on offline navigation-world-model datasets. Only a subset of the long-horizon prediction numbers is included (16s); other horizons and datasets are in the tables. Zero-shot Go Stanford results appear only as figures.
results: AR Forcing lowers LPIPS/DreamSim/FID versus NWM at almost all horizons on RECON, TartanDrive and SCAND. For 2s planning, ATE is 1.22 vs NWM 1.38 and PosErr 1.66 vs 1.85; at 16s it beats Self Forcing on most metrics. On HuRoN at 8-16s, visual metrics are worse than NWM (FID 99.6 vs 84.2 at 16s).
limitations: Gains are not universal: HuRoN long-horizon visual metrics and some YawErr/16s values are worse than NWM, and the paper does not use the full HuRoN dataset for privacy reasons; zero-shot Go Stanford is only shown qualitatively.
Stop-gradient rollouts are only an approximation of the true rollout objective, and no closed-loop real-robot or simulator navigation success is reported.
